Simulation study: do the weights recover known effects?

Source: vignettes/articles/simulations.Rmd
simulations.Rmd

This article checks, by simulation, whether the new features of ipw do what they should: each scenario generates data in which the true causal effect is known, estimates it, and repeats this hundreds of times, in the spirit of the simulated example in the JSS paper (van der Wal & Geskus 2011).

Main findings

  • The new weights remove confounding when their model is correct. Naive analyses and weights from misspecified models are biased by 15% to over 200%; the new weights reduce this to 0 to 5%.
  • The remaining small biases (3 to 5%) are properties of inverse probability weighting, not of the implementation. Weights computed from the true model (oracle weights) have the same bias for log-normal doses, and for smooth terms and ordinal exposures the bias shrinks as the sample grows.
  • ipwboot() gives accurate standard errors when the weights are well behaved, where robust standard errors are 8 to 10% too large. It does not fix analyses with extreme weights: with poor overlap or long products of time-varying weights, no standard error reaches 95% coverage, and the bootstrap is then not better than the robust standard error.

How the results were produced. The study is in dev/simulation-study.R; the code below shows the essential lines of each scenario. It takes about 20 minutes on 4 cores, so this page shows saved results. To reproduce them, run Rscript dev/simulation-study.R in the package folder (seed 20261101, L’Ecuyer random numbers, 4 parallel workers), or start the simulations workflow from the GitHub Actions tab. Replications: 500 for scenarios 1 to 4, 250 for 5 and 6, 200 for the large-sample and oracle checks, 1000 for 7a and 7b, and 500 for 7c and 7d, each with 200 bootstrap samples.

Reading the tables. Bias is the mean estimate minus the truth. The MCSE (Monte Carlo standard error) shows how precisely the simulation estimates that bias: a bias within about 2 MCSE of 0 could be simulation noise. Empirical SD is the spread of the estimates; RMSE combines bias and spread.

1. ATE, ATT and overlap weights, and ipwprob()

The effect of a binary exposure varies with the confounder l, so the three estimands differ. Their true values, from 2 million simulated people, are ATE = 1.00, ATT = 1.27 and ATO = 0.86. Each weighting scheme is compared with its own target; ipwprob() is given the true propensity scores.

d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
d$a <- rbinom(1000, 1, plogis(0.5 + 0.8 * d$l))
d$y <- d$a * (1 + d$l) + d$l + rnorm(1000)
w.att <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  denominator = ~ l, data = d, estimand = "ATT")$ipw.weights
coef(lm(y ~ a, data = d, weights = w.att))["a"]
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted (target ATE) 0.999 1.981 0.982 0.005 0.112 0.988 500
ATE weights 0.999 1.003 0.004 0.004 0.080 0.080 500
ATT weights (target ATT) 1.275 1.283 0.008 0.004 0.099 0.099 500
ATO weights (target ATO) 0.861 0.863 0.002 0.003 0.078 0.078 500
ipwprob, true probabilities (ATE) 0.999 1.006 0.007 0.006 0.139 0.139 500

All weighted estimates are within 1% of their own estimand; the unweighted difference is twice the ATE.

2. Count exposures: Poisson or negative binomial

Each extra unit of a count exposure raises the outcome by 0.5. In 2a the counts are overdispersed (negative binomial); in 2b they are Poisson.

d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(1000))
d$v <- rnbinom(1000, size = 2, mu = exp(0.5 + 0.4 * d$l))   # 2b: rpois(1000, exp(0.5 + 0.4 * d$l))
d$y <- 0.5 * d$v + d$l + rnorm(1000)
w.nb <- ipwpoint(exposure = v, family = "negbin", numerator = ~ 1,
                 denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 0.5 0.670 0.170 0.001 0.022 0.171 500
poisson weights (misspecified) 0.5 0.336 -0.164 0.003 0.068 0.178 500
negbin weights (correct) 0.5 0.507 0.007 0.002 0.035 0.035 500
unweighted 0.5 0.805 0.305 0.001 0.028 0.307 500
poisson weights (correct) 0.5 0.507 0.007 0.003 0.062 0.063 500
negbin weights (also valid: theta large) 0.5 0.518 0.018 0.003 0.064 0.066 500

With the correct model, both families are within 1.5% of the truth. The Poisson model applied to overdispersed counts over-corrects as strongly as the unweighted analysis under-corrects. The negative binomial model remains usable for Poisson data (bias 3.6%), so it is the safer choice when in doubt.

3. Skewed continuous exposures: gaussian, gamma or log-normal

One unit of dose raises the outcome by 1. In 3a the dose is log-normal given l, in 3b gamma. In 3a the true densities are known, so oracle weights (the true marginal density over the true conditional density) show what weighting can achieve without any estimation error; they are also computed for a 5 times larger sample.

d <- data.frame(l = rnorm(2000))
d$dose <- exp(0.5 + 0.5 * d$l + rnorm(2000, 0, 0.6))   # 3b: rgamma(2000, 3, 3 / exp(0.5 + 0.3 * d$l))
d$y <- d$dose + 2 * d$l + rnorm(2000)
w.ln <- ipwpoint(exposure = dose, family = "lognormal", numerator = ~ 1,
                 denominator = ~ l, data = d)$ipw.weights
oracle <- dlnorm(d$dose, 0.5, sqrt(0.61)) / dlnorm(d$dose, 0.5 + 0.5 * d$l, 0.6)
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.537 0.537 0.002 0.041 0.538 500
gaussian weights (misspecified) 1 1.120 0.120 0.015 0.344 0.363 493
gamma weights (misspecified) 1 0.963 -0.037 0.008 0.177 0.181 500
lognormal weights (correct), n = 2000 1 1.050 0.050 0.004 0.096 0.108 500
lognormal weights (correct), n = 10000 1 1.034 0.034 0.005 0.065 0.073 200
lognormal weights, truncated 1% 1 1.179 0.179 0.002 0.038 0.183 500
oracle weights (true densities), n = 2000 1 1.049 0.049 0.005 0.104 0.115 500
oracle weights (true densities), n = 10000 1 1.032 0.032 0.005 0.067 0.074 200
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.758 0.758 0.002 0.040 0.759 500
gaussian weights (misspecified) 1 1.142 0.142 0.004 0.079 0.162 500
gamma weights (correct) 1 1.032 0.032 0.005 0.111 0.115 500
lognormal weights (misspecified) 1 1.024 0.024 0.010 0.220 0.221 500

The correct family removes most of the confounding (unweighted bias 54% and 76%). The 3 to 5% that remains is the same for oracle weights (5.0% vs 4.9% at n = 2000, 3.4% vs 3.2% at n = 10000), so it does not come from estimating the model: it is the finite-sample bias of weighting with densities of a skewed exposure, whose density ratios have a heavy tail, and it shrinks slowly as the sample grows. The gaussian model is clearly worse, and in 7 of 500 replications gave infinite weights, which ipwpoint() refuses. A misspecified skewed family (gamma for log-normal data or the reverse) has a small bias but up to twice the spread. Truncation reduces the spread a lot but adds bias.

4. Curved propensity: smooth terms with mgcv

The probability of exposure depends on l through a sine curve; the true effect is 2. Oracle weights use the true propensity.

d <- data.frame(l = runif(2000, -2, 2))
d$a <- rbinom(2000, 1, plogis(2 * sin(1.5 * d$l)))
d$y <- 2 * d$a + 3 * sin(1.5 * d$l) + rnorm(2000)
w.gam <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit",
                  numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ s(l), data = d)$ipw.weights
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 2 4.553 2.553 0.004 0.090 2.554 500
linear logistic weights (misspecified) 2 2.662 0.662 0.004 0.079 0.667 500
s(l) weights, n = 2000 2 2.072 0.072 0.003 0.062 0.095 500
s(l) weights, n = 10000 2 2.031 0.031 0.002 0.026 0.040 200
oracle weights (true propensity), n = 2000 2 2.014 0.014 0.007 0.148 0.149 500
oracle weights (true propensity), n = 10000 2 1.993 -0.007 0.005 0.065 0.066 200

A straight-line logistic model leaves a quarter of the confounding bias. With s(l) the bias is 3.6% at n = 2000 and 1.5% at n = 10000: it halves as the sample grows five-fold, as expected for a smoothing estimate that approaches the true curve. Oracle weights are unbiased, which confirms that the remaining bias comes from estimating the curve.

5. Time-varying exposure, type = "all"

5a. Ordinal dose

A dose level (0, 1, 2) is chosen at each of 4 visits from a proportional-odds model given the confounder L and the previous dose. L is affected by the previous dose and by an unmeasured U that also affects the outcome; the outcome rises by 1 per unit of cumulative dose. This is the situation in the JSS paper where ordinary adjustment fails.

for (t in 1:4) {
  l <- U + 0.4 * prev + rnorm(n, 0, 0.5)
  dose <- findInterval(0.8 * l + 0.6 * prev + rlogis(n), c(0, 1.5))   # 0, 1, 2
  prev <- dose
}
y <- cumulative.dose + 2 * U + rnorm(n)
w <- ipwtm(exposure = dose, family = "ordinal", link = "logit",
           numerator = ~ dose.lag, denominator = ~ dose.lag + l,
           id = id, timevar = time, type = "all", data = long)
# weight at the last visit, then lm(y ~ cumulative.dose, weights = ...)
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.490 0.490 0.002 0.034 0.491 250
regression adjustment for L 1 0.856 -0.144 0.002 0.029 0.147 250
ordinal weights (correct), 500 people 1 1.025 0.025 0.008 0.122 0.124 250
ordinal weights (correct), 2500 people 1 1.014 0.014 0.005 0.073 0.074 200
multinomial weights, 500 people 1 1.007 0.007 0.008 0.133 0.133 250
oracle weights (true probabilities, unstabilized), 500 people 1 1.007 0.007 0.010 0.152 0.152 250
oracle weights (true probabilities, unstabilized), 2500 people 1 1.008 0.008 0.006 0.083 0.084 200

Both naive analyses are biased (+49% and -14%). Ordinal and multinomial weights recover the effect; the 2.5% bias of the ordinal weights at 500 people falls to 1.4% at 2500, and oracle weights are within 1%.

5b. Smooth terms in ipwtm()

A binary exposure is chosen at each visit with a curved effect of L (logit = -0.3 + 2 sin(1.5 L) + 0.6 × previous exposure), in the same design.

w <- ipwtm(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit", numerator = ~ a.lag,
           denominator = ~ a.lag + s(l), id = id, timevar = time, type = "all", data = long)
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.651 0.651 0.004 0.061 0.654 250
linear logistic weights (misspecified) 1 -0.152 -1.152 0.033 0.526 1.266 250
s(l) weights 1 1.055 0.055 0.015 0.243 0.249 250

Here a straight-line model is worse than no weighting at all: its weights turn the effect of +1 into a negative estimate. With s(l) the bias is 5.5%.

6. Recurrent exposure events, family = "survival", type = "all"

6a and 6b. Weights against the true weights

Exposure events (for example new prescriptions) happen repeatedly with a known proportional hazard: baseline 2 per unit time, log hazard ratio 0.5 for a fixed covariate x and -1 for a time-varying covariate xt. Because the true hazard is known, the true weights are known too. In 6a all people share a grid of 10 intervals (as in haartdat); in 6b the events happen in continuous time, xt changes at different times for each person, and each event ends an interval (start-stop data cut at events, as in Graffeo et al. 2018).

w <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", denominator = ~ x + xt,
           id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "all", data = d)
coef(w$den.mod)
median(abs(log(w$ipw.weights / true.weights)))
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
Cox coefficient of x 0.5 0.500 0.000 0.006 0.088 0.088 250
Cox coefficient of xt -1.0 -1.007 -0.007 0.007 0.118 0.118 250
median |log(estimated / true weight)| 0.0 0.074 0.074 0.001 0.022 0.077 250
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
Cox coefficient of x 0.5 0.506 0.006 0.005 0.084 0.084 250
Cox coefficient of xt -1.0 -0.990 0.010 0.007 0.104 0.104 250
median |log(estimated / true weight)| 0.0 0.090 0.090 0.001 0.022 0.092 250

The Cox coefficients are unbiased in both designs, and the estimated weights are typically within 7 to 9% of the true weights, which is the estimation noise of the baseline hazard.

6c. Causal effect of the number of exposure events

Exposure events happen in continuous time with hazard 1.5 exp(0.6 L). L is updated at 4 visits, is lowered by earlier events (as treatment raising CD4 lowers the need for more) and depends on an unmeasured U that also affects the outcome. The outcome rises by 1 per event.

w <- ipwtm(exposure = expo, family = "survival", numerator = ~ 1, denominator = ~ l,
           id = id, tstart = tstart, timevar = fuptime, type = "all", data = d)
# weight at each person's last row, then lm(y ~ number.of.events, weights = ...)
Method Truth Mean estimate Bias MCSE of bias Empirical SD RMSE Replications
unweighted 1 1.799 0.799 0.004 0.060 0.801 250
regression adjustment for L 1 1.220 0.220 0.003 0.047 0.224 250
survival type all weights 1 1.034 0.034 0.012 0.193 0.196 250

The weights reduce the bias from 80% (unweighted) and 22% (adjustment for L) to 3.4%. The method of Graffeo et al. uses, for an interval ending in an event, the probability of an event during that interval; this simulation shows that the approximation works for estimating a causal effect.

7. Standard errors: ipwboot(), robust and naive

Each table shows the mean estimated standard error divided by the actual spread of the estimates (1 is ideal) and the coverage of 95% confidence intervals.

7a and 7b. Linear MSM for a binary exposure

True effect 10, n = 500, stabilized weights. In 7a, exposure probabilities are mostly between 0.1 and 0.9 (good overlap); 7b is the simulated example of the JSS paper, where many people are almost certain to be exposed or unexposed.

msm.effect <- function(dd) {
  w <- ipwpoint(exposure = a, family = "binomial", link = "logit", numerator = ~ 1,
                denominator = ~ l, data = dd)$ipw.weights
  coef(lm(y ~ a, data = dd, weights = w))["a"]
}
ipwboot(d, msm.effect, R = 200)
Method Mean estimate Mean SE Empirical SD SE / empirical SD Coverage of 95% CI MCSE of coverage Replications
ipwboot, percentile CI 9.981 0.492 0.487 1.011 0.936 0.008 1000
ipwboot SE, Wald CI 9.981 0.492 0.487 1.011 0.947 0.007 1000
robust SE (svyglm), Wald CI 9.981 0.536 0.487 1.101 0.967 0.006 1000
Method Mean estimate Mean SE Empirical SD SE / empirical SD Coverage of 95% CI MCSE of coverage Replications
ipwboot, percentile CI 11.019 1.110 1.787 0.621 0.560 0.016 1000
ipwboot SE, Wald CI 11.019 1.110 1.787 0.621 0.585 0.016 1000
robust SE (svyglm), Wald CI 11.019 1.113 1.787 0.623 0.591 0.016 1000

With good overlap the bootstrap standard error is accurate (ratio 1.01, Wald coverage 94.7%), while the robust standard error is 10% too large (coverage 96.7%), in line with Austin (2016); percentile intervals cover slightly less than 95%. In the JSS example the estimate itself is biased (11.0 instead of 10) and all standard errors are 38% too small, so coverage is below 60% whatever method is used.

7c. Weighted Cox MSM

Austin (2016) studied weighted Cox models. Here event times are exponential with hazard 0.1 exp(-0.7 a + 0.8 l), censored at 5; n = 1000. The true marginal log hazard ratio, -0.624, is computed from both potential outcomes of 200,000 people (it differs from -0.7 because hazard ratios are not collapsible).

Method Mean estimate Mean SE Empirical SD SE / empirical SD Coverage of 95% CI MCSE of coverage Replications
naive SE (coxph), Wald CI -0.61 0.117 0.113 1.037 0.952 0.010 500
robust SE (coxph), Wald CI -0.61 0.122 0.113 1.078 0.960 0.009 500
ipwboot SE, Wald CI -0.61 0.110 0.113 0.974 0.936 0.011 500
ipwboot, percentile CI -0.61 0.110 0.113 0.974 0.934 0.011 500

All three standard errors are close to the truth here. The robust standard error is again too large (+8%); the naive one (+4%) and the bootstrap (-3%) are within simulation noise of 1. With stabilized weights and good overlap, the bootstrap therefore brings no clear gain over the naive standard error in this setting.

7d. Time-varying exposure, bootstrap by person

The design of scenario 5 with a binary exposure; ipwboot(id = id) resamples people with all their visits.

ipwboot(long, tv.effect, id = id, R = 200)
Method Mean estimate Mean SE Empirical SD SE / empirical SD Coverage of 95% CI MCSE of coverage Replications
ipwboot (id), percentile CI 1.033 0.146 0.222 0.658 0.778 0.019 500
ipwboot (id) SE, Wald CI 1.033 0.146 0.222 0.658 0.792 0.018 500
robust SE (svyglm), Wald CI 1.033 0.163 0.222 0.737 0.838 0.016 500

Neither method is adequate here: the bootstrap standard error is 34% too small and the robust one 26% too small, with coverage of 79% and 84%. The weights are products over 4 visits, so a few people get very large weights and the estimate has a heavy-tailed distribution that 500 people do not represent well, the same problem as in 7b. Truncation, a larger sample or a better-balanced design would be needed; the bootstrap does not repair it.

Conclusions

The simulations support the new models: with the correct model, each of them removes nearly all confounding, and the small biases that remain are either shared by weights from the true model or shrink with the sample size. They support ipwboot() for analyses with well-behaved weights, where it gives accurate standard errors and robust standard errors are conservative. They also show its limit: when weights are extreme (poor overlap, long products of time-varying weights), no standard error is reliable, and the first step is to examine the weights (summary(), ipwplot()) and consider overlap weights, truncation or a different model.

References

  • Austin PC (2016). Variance estimation when using inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) with survival analysis. Statistics in Medicine 35, 5642-5655.
  • Graffeo N, Latouche A, Geskus RB, Chevret S (2018). Modeling time-varying exposure using inverse probability of treatment weights. Biometrical Journal 60, 323-332.
  • Li F, Morgan KL, Zaslavsky AM (2018). Balancing covariates via propensity score weighting. Journal of the American Statistical Association 113, 390-400.
  • van der Wal WM, Geskus RB (2011). ipw: An R package for inverse probability weighting. Journal of Statistical Software 43(13), 1-23.
